title: Cartesian base-equivalence invariance and extension
statement:
Use cartesian fibrations over arbitrary small simplicial sets and their natural markings (the cartesian edges), as defined for arbitrary bases in [lem-coef-relative-marked-anodyne-calculus], and categorical equivalences, defined by tests $h\operatorname{Fun}(-,C)$ against all quasicategories, as in [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure].

For a small simplicial set $B$, let $\mathsf M_B$ be the category of marked simplicial sets with a map to $B$ and marking-preserving maps over $B$. Write $W_B$ for the maps inducing weak homotopy equivalences on $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_B(-,Q^\natural)$ for every cartesian fibration $Q\to B$. Assume the following family of structures is given in each universe: each $\mathsf M_B$ is a left proper combinatorial simplicial model category, its cofibrations are the underlying simplicial monomorphisms, its weak equivalences are $W_B$, and its fibrant objects are exactly $Q^\natural$ for cartesian fibrations $Q\to B$. Its mapping objects are $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_B$, and its simplicial tensor is $U\times K^\sharp$. Assume that a map between these fibrant objects belongs to $W_B$ if and only if it induces equivalences on all vertex fibers, equivalently if it has a marked inverse up to paths in the sharp mapping complexes. For every simplicial map $c:B\to D$, assume composition $c_!$ and pullback $c^*$ form a Quillen adjunction. The structures and their factorizations are formed in the input universe. Under these hypotheses the following statements hold.

(1) If $q:Z\to S$ is a cartesian fibration and $a:T\to S$ is a categorical equivalence of small simplicial sets, the projection $T\times_S Z\to Z$ is a categorical equivalence. No quasicategory hypothesis on $S$ or $T$ is imposed.

(2) If $i:S\to S'$ is a categorical equivalence of small simplicial sets and $q:Z\to S$ is a cartesian fibration, there exist a cartesian fibration $q':Z'\to S'$ and a cartesian-edge-preserving map $u:Z\to S\times_{S'}Z'$ over $S$ such that, for every small simplicial map $b:T\to S$, the induced map $T\times_S Z\to T\times_{S'}Z'$ is a categorical equivalence. The latter map uses $i b:T\to S'$ on the right. The universal comparison in (2) is required after every base change, with no fibrancy hypothesis on $T$.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.1.2 and Proposition 3.3.1.3, with Proposition 3.3.1.1 and Theorem 3.2.0.1 for their proof. The already constructed Cartesian model structures and base-change Quillen adjunctions used in that proof are explicit hypotheses here. The universal form of (2) follows by retaining the marked homotopy inverse of the equivalence in Corollary 3.3.1.2 under pullback. Read from HTT-second-reading.pdf in the delivery sandbox; no Stacks tag states this simplicial result.

proof.text:
Work in one input universe, enlarging only to form localizations. Write $\mathsf M=\mathsf M_{\Delta^0}$; its cofibrations and weak equivalences coincide with the absolute marked model of [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], so its fibrations coincide too by the lifting characterization. For each $S$, define $L_S$ by the canonical marked cone formula of [lem-coef-marked-cone-generator-calculations], indexed by $I_S=\mathfrak C[S]^{\mathrm{op}}$. The projective model on $\mathsf M^{I_S}$ exists without requiring $I_S$ locally Kan. The cone construction preserves colimits: a cone diagram is presented by the simplices and marked edges of its input, with face, degeneracy and composition relations; taking a colimit takes the same generators and relations. Construct $U_S$ explicitly: an $n$-simplex over $\sigma:\Delta^n\to S$ is a marked enriched natural map $L_S((\Delta^n)^\flat_\sigma)\to F$; mark an edge if its map extends across $L_S((\Delta^1)^\flat_\sigma)\to L_S((\Delta^1)^\sharp_\sigma)$. Such an extension, if present, is unique, since only markings change. Simplexwise decomposition gives the actual adjunction $L_S\dashv U_S$. For $a:A\to B$, cone substitution gives
$$L_Ba_!\cong(\mathfrak C[a]^{\mathrm{op}})_!L_A.$$
Both sides present the same cone generators after enriched left Kan extension; their markings are generated by the same precomposites. Substitution at a vertex similarly identifies $(U_SF)_s=U_0(F(s))$, where $T=L_{\Delta^0}$ and $U_0$ is its right adjoint. The fiber restriction of an adjoint map $X\to U_SF$ is adjoint to $T(X_s)\to L_SX(s)\to F(s)$. These are adjunction bijections on actual simplices, not merely identifications on objects.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.1.4 and Corollary 3.2.1.5; vertex adjunction in Lemma 3.2.3.2

proof.text: Every marked monomorphism is built by adjoining missing simplices by $(\partial\Delta^n)^\flat\to(\Delta^n)^\flat$, then missing markings by $(\Delta^1)^\flat\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp$. The cone generator calculations, followed by the substitutions of step 1, send these to projective cofibrations. Enriched left Kan extension preserves projective cofibrations and trivial cofibrations because its right adjoint preserves the objectwise fibrations and trivial fibrations. The same generator calculations send every marked-anodyne generator over its own base to a projective trivial cofibration. Colimit preservation and weak saturation therefore show that $L_S$ preserves monomorphisms and sends marked-anodyne maps to projective trivial cofibrations. We also need replacements without invoking the relative-model theorem that cites the present item: apply the small-object factorization to the small marked-anodyne generators with every map of their codomain to $S$. Domains are countable; for a continuous $\aleph_1$-chain of monomorphisms every map from a countable domain, and every equality between two such maps, occurs before one stage. The smallness hypothesis is satisfied. The resulting marked-anodyne $V\to RV$ has naturally marked Cartesian target by the relative lifting criterion. Relative mapping restriction makes this map an element of $W_S$. All constructions stay in the input universe.

source.place: Propositions 3.2.1.7 and 3.2.1.11; Remark 3.1.1.10 and the small-object construction

proof.text: Put $K=(\Delta^1)^\sharp$. The external-product cone comparison gives an objectwise weak equivalence $L_S(V\times K)\to L_S(V)\times T(K)$, compatible with projection to $L_S(V)$, and $T(K)=K$ by the edge calculation. The map $K\to\Delta^0$ is a point-model weak equivalence: the inclusion of the $1$-vertex $(\Delta^0)^\flat\hookrightarrow K$ is a marked-anodyne generator and its retraction is weak by two-out-of-three. Product preservation in $\mathsf M$ makes $L_S(V)\times K\to L_S(V)$ objectwise weak. Consequently $L_S(V\times K)\to L_S(V)$ is weak. Its two endpoint sections are the same inverse after localization. Thus $L_S$ sends a sharp marked homotopy to equality in the homotopy category. If $f$ is a weak equivalence between fibrant relative objects, the marked inverse and homotopies assumed in the item imply that $L_S(f)$ becomes invertible after localization; model localization detects weak equivalences, so $L_S(f)$ is objectwise weak. For general $f:V\to W$ in $W_S$, replace $V$ by $V'$ using step 2, and replace $W\amalg_V V'$ by $W'$ using step 2. Both $V\to V'$ and $W\to W'$ are marked anodyne, while $V'\to W'$ is a weak equivalence between fibrant objects by two-out-of-three. Step 2 handles the two replacement arrows and the preceding argument handles $V'\to W'$. Two-out-of-three now proves $L_S(f)$ weak. Hence $L_S\dashv U_S$ is Quillen. Its derived adjunction has the actual unit and counit with replacements, by the derived-adjunction lemma.

We next establish the point equivalence without citing the circular full straightening node. The cone generator calculation gives a natural marked augmentation $\alpha:T\to\mathrm{id}$, an isomorphism on a point and on both markings of an edge. For the spine inclusion $j:\operatorname{Sp}[n]\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$, [lem-cbc-spine-inner-anodyne] says it lifts against every inner fibration. Factor it by attaching all inner-horn problems over $\Delta^n$ countably often. Finite domains ensure the remaining map is an inner fibration. A lift exhibits $j$ as a retract of the inner-horn cell inclusion, so $j^\flat$ is marked anodyne. It and $T(j^\flat)$ are weak by the relative mapping criterion over a point and step 2. Since the spine is glued from vertices and edges and both functors preserve this gluing, $\alpha$ is an isomorphism on the spine. Naturality and two-out-of-three give that $\alpha_{(\Delta^n)^\flat}$ is weak for all $n$, including $n=0$.

Extend the preceding conclusion to all marked $V$. All objects of $\mathsf M$ are cofibrant, and $T$ preserves cofibrations by step 2. Induct over the finite boundary-cell construction of $\partial\Delta^n$, and then over the skeletal construction of an arbitrary underlying simplicial set with minimal marking. At a successor stage the two functors give a map of attaching spans with three weak component maps; the attaching legs on both sides are cofibrations. The coproduct and pushout assertions (a),(b) of [lem-coef-model-cofibrant-colimit-comparison] give the next weak comparison. At the countable union of skeleta, assertion (c) applies to the two continuous sequences of cofibrations. Finally adjoin the chosen markings by the marked-edge cells, where the augmentation is already an isomorphism on each of the two edge objects; assertions (a),(b) apply again. Both functors preserve these colimits. Thus $\alpha_V$ is weak for every $V$, also for $V=\varnothing$. As $T$ is left Quillen and every object is cofibrant, its left derived functor is naturally isomorphic to the identity. Its right derived adjoint is therefore an inverse: the adjunction bijections and triangle identities identify an adjoint to an equivalence with its inverse. This proves the point Quillen equivalence, with its actual adjoint maps.

For a naturally marked Cartesian $X\to S$, choose a projectively fibrant replacement $L_SX\to F$. Its adjoint is $j:X\to U_SF$, whose target is relative fibrant since $U_S$ is right Quillen. At a vertex $s$, the adjoint of $j_s$ under the point adjunction is exactly
$$T(X_s^+)\xrightarrow{\psi_{X,s}}L_SX(s)\longrightarrow F(s).$$
The first arrow is weak by [lem-coef-cartesian-cone-fiber-comparison], the second by replacement. The point Quillen equivalence of step 5 makes $j_s$ weak in $\mathsf M$. Both marked vertex fibers are point-fibrant by relative base change; their weak equivalence is an equivalence of quasicategories by the assumed vertex-fiber criterion at a point. The assumed fiber criterion over $S$ therefore gives $j\in W_S$. Thus the derived unit of $L_S\dashv U_S$ is invertible on all fibrant objects and hence on all objects after fibrant replacement, using step 3 and naturality.

source.place: Theorem 3.2.0.1, vertex restriction of its derived unit; the comparison defined before Lemma 3.2.3.3

proof.text: The right derived $U_S$ is conservative. For an actual map $g:F\to G$ between projectively fibrant diagrams, if $U_Sg$ is weak then the assumed fiber criterion and $(U_Sg)_s=U_0(g(s))$ make every $U_0(g(s))$ weak. The point equivalence then makes every $g(s)$ weak. This detects all localized morphisms: a morphism between fibrant diagrams is represented by a map from a projectively cofibrant replacement of its source to its fibrant target, by the simplicial-model mapping-space theorem. That replacement remains fibrant, since its map to the fibrant source is a trivial fibration. Localization detects weak equivalences, so the same test applies to that representative. The triangle identity says that the right derived image of the counit is inverse to the unit at the right-adjoint image. Step 6 and conservativity make the counit invertible as well. Consequently the canonical $L_S\dashv U_S$ is a Quillen equivalence for every small $S$. This establishes it from the explicitly assumed model structures and the cone-fiber computation.

source.place: Lemma 3.2.3.2 and the unit/counit test in Theorem 3.2.0.1

proof.text: Let $i:S\to S'$ be a categorical equivalence. Rigidification detection says $\mathfrak C[i]$ is Dwyer--Kan; so is its opposite, since taking opposite reverses the hom categories without changing their underlying mapping spaces. The enriched projective change-of-index theorem makes $(\mathfrak C[i]^{\mathrm{op}})_!$ a Quillen equivalence, with no local Kan restriction on either index. The natural isomorphism from step 1 identifies $L_{S'}i_!$ with $(\mathfrak C[i]^{\mathrm{op}})_!L_S$. All three cone and change-of-index derived functors on the other sides are equivalences by step 7 and the projective theorem. Hence the left derived $i_!$ is an equivalence by two-out-of-three. The assumed Quillen adjunction $i_!\dashv i^*$ and its derived adjunction then imply that its derived unit and counit are invertible. This is Proposition 3.3.1.1 under precisely the hypotheses of the item.

Apply the fibrant replacement in $\mathsf M_{S'}$ to $i_!Z^
atural$, obtaining a weak equivalence $i_!Z^
atural	o (Z')^
atural$ with $Z'	o S'$ Cartesian. Every object of $\mathsf M_S$ is cofibrant, so the adjoint map
$$u:Z^
atural\longrightarrow i^*((Z')^
atural)$$
represents the derived unit at $Z^
atural$. Step 8 and detection by localization make $u\in W_S$. Both its source and target are fibrant, the latter by relative pullback. By the hypothesis of the item choose a marked inverse $v$ over $S$ and sharp mapping-complex paths $vu\simeq1$ and $uv\simeq1$. In particular $u$ preserves Cartesian edges. This constructs the actual map required by (2), before checking its universal comparison.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.1.2, retaining an actual representative of the derived unit

proof.text: For any $b:T\to S$, degreewise pullback retains $u,v$ and their sharp homotopies: $T\times_S(Z\times(\Delta^1)^\sharp)=(T\times_SZ)\times(\Delta^1)^\sharp$ over $T$, with identical product markings. The pulled-back objects are naturally marked Cartesian fibrations by the relative base-change statement. Forgetting markings, these inverse data give a categorical equivalence even when $T$ is not a quasicategory. Here is the test: each component of a pulled-back homotopy is a marked edge over a degenerate base edge. Restricting to its vertex fiber makes it an equivalence, since a naturally marked Cartesian fibration over a point is precisely a point-fibrant marked quasicategory. Any map from the total space to a test quasicategory $C$ sends that component to an equivalence in $C$. The pointwise equivalence criterion for $\operatorname{Fun}(-,C)$ therefore turns the homotopies into natural equivalences. Precomposition by the two underlying maps consequently gives inverse equivalences of $h\operatorname{Fun}(-,C)$, exactly the categorical-equivalence test. Thus $b^*u:T\times_SZ\to T\times_{S'}Z'$ is a categorical equivalence for every small $T$, proving all of (2).

source.place: Corollary 3.3.1.2 and the homotopy-inverse alternative in Proposition 3.3.1.5

proof.text:
Use the mapping simplex of [lem-coef-mapping-simplex-final-edge], marking edges $(\alpha,s_0a)$. Prove by induction on $n$ that every marked $s:A^\flat\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp\to Y^\natural$ over a Cartesian $Y\to\Delta^n$ extends through a marked $f:M(A_0\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow A_n)\to Y^\natural$, with every vertex-fiber map categorical. Factor $A\to Y_n$ as a monomorphism $A\hookrightarrow A_n$ followed by a trivial Kan fibration $h:A_n\to Y_n$. The latter lifts all monomorphisms, hence is also a Joyal trivial fibration. Apply [lem-coef-cartesian-mapping-simplex-prism-extension] to obtain a marked prism on $A_n$ extending $s$ and equal to $h$ at the final vertex. For $n=0$ this is the presentation. For $n>0$, restrict that prism to $\Delta^{\{0,\ldots,n-1\}}$ and apply the induction hypothesis with input $A_n$. It supplies the shorter chain and a map $A_n\to A_{n-1}$. The degreewise formula gives
$$M(A_\bullet)=M(A_0\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow A_{n-1})\amalg_{A_n\times\Delta^{n-1}}(A_n\times\Delta^n).$$
The two maps agree on the displayed intersection, including markings, so glue to $f$. The earlier fibers are equivalences by induction and the final one by $h$. Taking $A=\varnothing$ supplies a presentation for every $Y$.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2.11 and its proof (printed pp. 184–185): final-fiber factorization, marked-anodyne extension f_0 and induction; mapping simplex and its marking as defined before Remark 3.2.2.1 and in Notation 3.2.2.3, with the pullback description of Remark 3.2.2.2

proof.text:
Every fiberwise-equivalent marked presentation $f:M(A_\bullet)\to Y$ is categorical, by induction on $n$; for $n=0$ this is its fiber equivalence. Let $M_-$ and $Y_-$ be the restrictions to vertices below $n$. In coherent realization, the full subcategories below $n$ are $\mathfrak C[M_-]$ and $\mathfrak C[Y_-]$, and the final full subcategories are $\mathfrak C[A_n]$ and $\mathfrak C[Y_n]$. Indeed each generating simplex lies over a nondecreasing sequence in $[n]$, and composition concatenates such sequences. A path ending below $n$ never reaches $n$; a path beginning at $n$ remains there. This also shows there are no maps from the final part back to the earlier part. The unmixed maps are weak equivalences by induction and the final-fiber equivalence, using rigidification detection. For $x$ below $n$ and $y\in A_n$, take the final transition $e:y'\to y$ of [lem-coef-mapping-simplex-final-edge]. In the commutative postcomposition square, the top arrow
$$\mathfrak C[M](x,y')\longrightarrow\mathfrak C[M](x,y)$$
is weak by that node. The bottom arrow in $\mathfrak C[Y]$ is weak by [lem-coef-cartesian-mapping-simplex-mixed-mapping-equivalence], with $z=f(x)$, $a=f(y')$, $b=f(y)$: the marked map makes $f(e)$ Cartesian, and $p(f(x))\leq n-1=p(f(y'))$. The left vertical map is weak by induction. Two-out-of-three makes the right vertical map weak. Finally every vertex of $Y$ is equivalent to an image vertex by the given fiber equivalences. Thus $\mathfrak C[f]$ is Dwyer–Kan and [lem-coef-rigidification-equivalence-detection] makes $f$ categorical.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2.10 and its proof (printed pp. 183–184), with Lemma 3.2.2.9 (printed pp. 182–183) for the top arrow of the mixed mapping-space square

proof.text: The map $f$ of step 12 remains categorical over every simplicial subset $K\subseteq\Delta^n$. First, pullback along a simplex $\alpha:\Delta^m\to\Delta^n$ identifies $M(A_\bullet)\times_{\Delta^n}\Delta^m$ with the mapping simplex of $A_{\alpha(0)}\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow A_{\alpha(m)}$ by its formula on $(\beta,a)$. The restricted map preserves the marked edges and has the same fiber equivalences; step 12 applies. For any subcomplex $K$, attach its finitely many nondegenerate simplices in increasing dimension. The two inverse images of a union $K_0\cup_{\partial\tau}\tau$ are degreewise pushouts of the inverse images of $K_0\leftarrow\partial\tau\to\tau$: membership in the two inverse-image subsets has exactly their inverse-image intersection. By induction the comparison on $K_0$ and $\partial\tau$ is weak, and the simplex comparison is weak by the preceding argument. All objects are Joyal-cofibrant and the two attaching legs are monomorphisms. Clause (b) of the cofibrant-colimit comparison proves the next weak map. The empty subcomplex gives the identity of the empty simplicial set. In particular both the full-simplex map and every inner-horn restriction of $f$ are categorical equivalences.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2.7(2), through Proposition 3.2.2.8; only the finite-subcomplex case is needed here.

proof.text: Fix an inner horn $\Lambda_i^n\subseteq\Delta^n$, $0<i<n$, and a Cartesian $Y\to\Delta^n$. Choose the presentation in step 11. Step 13 says its maps to $Y$ both before and after restriction to the horn are categorical equivalences. The inclusion $M(A_\bullet)|_{\Lambda_i^n}\hookrightarrow M(A_\bullet)$ is the pushout of $A_n\times\Lambda_i^n\hookrightarrow A_n\times\Delta^n$. To check this, the horn contains the final face $\Delta^{n-1}$, and $M(A_\bullet)=M_-\amalg_{A_n\times\Delta^{n-1}}(A_n\times\Delta^n)$; restricting this equality to the horn gives the asserted pushout. The product horn inclusion is inner anodyne by pushout-product with $\varnothing\hookrightarrow A_n$. It is a Joyal trivial cofibration: its left lifting property against inner fibrations implies the left lifting property against Joyal fibrations, since the latter lift inner horns; the model weak-factorization characterization then applies. Pushout preserves that left lifting property. Two-out-of-three in the presentation square shows $Y|_{\Lambda_i^n}\hookrightarrow Y$ categorical, and it is a monomorphism.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.1.3, first paragraph, printed p. 205; the mapping-simplex pushout is checked explicitly.

proof.text: For a fixed Cartesian $Z\to S$, this inner-horn result implies that pullback preserves every inner-anodyne map over $S$. Apply the small-object theorem to all inner-horn inclusions with maps of their codomains to $S$. Finite domains preserve the countable cell-chain colimits, so an inner-anodyne map is a retract of an inner-horn cell map (factor it, then lift against the remaining inner fibration). Degreewise pullback in sets preserves the coproducts and pushouts in the slice, as well as ordinal colimits: in degree $r$ these are computed separately in each fiber over $S_r$. Each pulled-back horn cell is a Joyal trivial cofibration by step 14 applied to the pullback Cartesian fibration over its attaching simplex. A coproduct, pushout, transfinite composite or retract of trivial cofibrations is still trivial: a compatible lift against a Joyal fibration is obtained separately on coproducts, by a pushout lift, successively along the ordinal, and then by a retract. This proves the inner-anodyne case of (1) without any quasicategory hypothesis on the bases.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.1.3, reduction to an inner horn; the weak-saturation reduction is written out.

proof.text: For later use, prove (1) when $a:T\to S$ is an equivalence between quasicategories. The relative calculus makes $Z$ a quasicategory and $q$ a Joyal fibration; the Joyal characterization makes it an isofibration. The isofibration pullback-limit theorem identifies $T\times_S Z$ with the pullback in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ by its actual projection square. The quasicategory characterization gives a quasi-inverse to $a$, so for every quasicategory $Q$ postcomposition by $a$ induces an equivalence on $\operatorname{Fun}(Q,-)$ and hence on their cores. The theorem's displayed mapping-space homotopy pullback then makes $\operatorname{Map}(Q,T\times_S Z)\to\operatorname{Map}(Q,Z)$ a weak homotopy equivalence: pullback along an equivalence of Kan complexes has this property by the Kan homotopy-pullback model and right properness. This detects an inverse to the specified projection $w$: take $Q=Z$ to obtain $g$ with $wg=1$ in $h\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$, then take $Q=T\times_S Z$ and use injectivity to get $gw=1$. Thus $w$ is an equivalence and hence a categorical equivalence by the Joyal characterization. This argument concerns only fibrant bases.

source.place: Corollary 2.4.4.5, printed p. 132; equivalently its fibrant-base homotopy-pullback argument.

proof.text:
Finally take arbitrary $a:T\to S$ in (1). By the inner-horn small-object construction choose $T\hookrightarrow T'$ inner anodyne with $T'$ a quasicategory, and then an inner-anodyne map $T'\amalg_T S\hookrightarrow S'$ with $S'$ a quasicategory. Thus $j:S\hookrightarrow S'$ is inner anodyne, and the induced $a':T'\to S'$ is categorical by two-out-of-three, since $a$ and both replacement inclusions are categorical. Apply (2), already proved in steps 9–10, to $j$ and $Z$: obtain $Z'\to S'$ and the fixed universally categorical map $Z\to S\times_{S'}Z'$. In the commutative square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}T\times_S Z&\longrightarrow&Z\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ T\times_{S'}Z'&\longrightarrow&S\times_{S'}Z',\end{array}$$
both vertical maps are categorical by step 10. The bottom horizontal map is categorical: its composite with $S\times_{S'}Z'\to Z'$ equals
$$T\times_{S'}Z'\longrightarrow T'\times_{S'}Z'\longrightarrow Z'.$$
The first map is categorical by step 15 applied to $T\hookrightarrow T'$ and the Cartesian fibration $T'\times_{S'}Z'\to T'$; the second is categorical by step 16 applied to $a'$. Also $S\times_{S'}Z'\to Z'$ is categorical by step 15 applied to $j$. Two-out-of-three gives the bottom horizontal equivalence, and the square gives the desired top one. All products use the displayed composite base maps; empty bases and empty fibers require no choices of vertices.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.1.3, second paragraph and comparison diagram, printed p. 206.

The hypothesis is needed (counterexample without it: Y=Delta^1, z=1). It is not a restatement of the intrinsic criterion.
